original.title: Shoulder to Waist Ratio: What the Number Really Means
original.description: Learn how to measure your shoulder to waist ratio, what studies actually show about the 1.6 ideal, and why your waist matters more than shoulder size.
original.h1_displayed: Shoulder to Waist Ratio: How to Measure It and What Actually Matters
original.body_markdown:
Spend a few minutes in any physique forum and you will see the same number: **1.618**. It is called the golden ratio, the Adonis index, the V-taper target. It is presented as the shoulder-to-waist proportion that makes a body look its best.

The real picture is more useful than the meme. Shoulder to waist ratio is a simple, trackable number. Studies do link a broader-shouldered, narrower-waisted torso with higher attractiveness ratings. But the best recent data does not point to 1.618. It also shows that one part of the equation does far more work than the other.

This guide covers how to measure your ratio properly, what the studies found, where the popular advice goes wrong, and how to improve the number in ways that also make sense for your training.

## What Shoulder to Waist Ratio Measures

Shoulder to waist ratio (often shortened to **SWR**) compares the circumference of your shoulders with the circumference of your waist. A higher number means your shoulders are wider relative to your waist. Visually, that reads as a V-shaped torso.

Researchers often study a close relative, the **shoulder-to-hip ratio (SHR)**. It compares shoulder circumference with hip circumference. Both ratios describe the same basic shape: wide on top, narrower lower down.

SHR is **sexually dimorphic**, meaning it differs on average between men and women. Men tend to have higher ratios than women, largely because of differences in upper-body muscle and frame.

### How to Calculate It

The formula is simple:

**Shoulder circumference ÷ waist circumference = shoulder to waist ratio**

If your shoulders measure 120 cm around and your waist measures 80 cm, your ratio is 1.50. Use the same unit for both measurements and the unit does not matter.

To see how demanding the popular targets are, work backwards from your waist. With an 80 cm waist:

- **A ratio of 1.57** requires shoulders of about 126 cm.
- **A ratio of 1.618** requires shoulders of about 129 cm.

That 3 cm gap is the difference between the number in the best recent study and the number repeated online.

## How to Measure Your Ratio Accurately

Your tape technique matters as much as your physique. A slightly tilted tape or a sucked-in stomach can move your ratio more than a month of training. Follow the same routine every time:

1. **Use a soft tailor's tape**, not a rigid metal tape.
2. **Stand tall and relaxed** with your arms hanging at your sides. Don't flare your lats or puff your chest.
3. **Measure your shoulders** around the widest point of your deltoids, the rounded muscles that cap each shoulder. Keep the tape level all the way around. A second person makes this much easier.
4. **Measure your waist** at the narrowest point of your torso, usually just above the belly button. Some guides use the navel instead. Pick one landmark and stick with it.
5. **Breathe out normally before measuring your waist.** Don't suck in, and don't push your stomach out.
6. **Take each measurement twice** and use the average if they differ.
7. **Measure under the same conditions each time**, ideally in the morning before eating, so day-to-day bloating doesn't distort your trend.

The measurement is most useful as a trend, not a one-off verdict. Recording it every few weeks tells you far more than a single reading.

## Where the 1.618 Golden Ratio Comes From

The golden ratio, roughly 1.618, is a mathematical proportion famous in art and architecture. Bodybuilding culture adopted it as the ideal V-taper. Classical statues and golden-era physiques are often held up as examples.

The problem is that the exact figure is a cultural convention, not a measured optimum. Many calculator sites and fitness articles repeat a version of the claim that women across cultures consistently pick 1.6 as the most attractive male shape. Those claims usually trace back to older or secondary sources rather than to recent data you can check.

Treat 1.618 as an aesthetic tradition. It is not a scientific target, and it is not a health standard.

## What the Research Actually Found

The evidence on shoulder and torso proportions is real, but more nuanced than the meme. Three findings matter most.

### Body Fat Outweighed the Ratio

One study used 15 **DXA images** of men. DXA, or dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, is a body scan that maps fat and lean tissue. The images varied in shoulder to waist ratio and body fat. Raters in China, Lithuania and the UK then ranked them for attractiveness.

According to the [study's published abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0191886925002028?_bhlid=221f41b196ca84546a6c2cdc8b8de4fb3dc31ae8), attractiveness peaked at an SWR of **around 1.57**. Above that peak, the relationship was very flat and variable.

The more important finding came when ratio and body fat were analysed together. **Adiposity (body fat) explained more of the variation in attractiveness ratings than the ratio did**, and this held in all three countries. A Psychology Today summary of the same work reports 283 participants. It also notes that waist size is closely tied to body fat levels.

The practical reading: a lean waist did more work than an extreme shoulder measurement.

### Both Waist and Shoulders Count

If body fat dominates, are shoulders irrelevant? No. A [University of Stirling manuscript on preferences for sexually dimorphic body traits](https://dspace.stir.ac.uk/bitstream/1893/30130/1/SPPS_20Manuscript_20Final.pdf) analysed several torso measures. It found that a higher shoulder-to-waist ratio had a positive effect on attractiveness *beyond* the effect of having a narrow waist alone. The influence of these ratios was stronger for male bodies than for female bodies.

In plain terms, a narrow waist on its own and broad shoulders on their own each fall short of the two combined.

### Bigger Is Not Automatically Better

An EEG study (EEG records electrical activity in the brain) found a consistent pattern in its rating task. [Larger shoulder-to-hip ratios were rated more attractive than smaller ones](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37170034/), regardless of the sex of the figure or the rater.

Other work on muscularity complicates the "more is better" reading. A paper testing why muscularity is rated attractive found that **men with moderate muscularity were rated most attractive**. Very lean, slender builds and very heavily muscled builds were rated lower. That fits the flat curve above 1.57 in the DXA study. Past a point, extra shoulder size adds little.

Two more caveats are worth knowing:

- **These studies measure perceived attractiveness of images or avatars.** They say nothing direct about health, and they don't capture individual taste.
- **Image-based ratios may not match your tape number.** Studies typically compare body shapes on screen, while you measure circumference with a tape. Use research figures as rough reference points, not as a pass mark for your own tape reading.

{{IMAGE_2}}

## Shoulder to Waist Ratio for Women

Most online targets for this ratio are written for men. Women deserve a straight answer rather than a borrowed number.

There is **no well-established target ratio for women** comparable to the figure cited for men. You will see a "1.4 for women" figure on calculator sites, but it traces back to the same secondary sources as the 1.618 claim. In the EEG study, women raters as well as men rated larger shoulder-to-hip ratios as more attractive on female figures too. Brain activity, however, did not change with the ratio for female avatars.

For women interested in proportions, the more relevant shape is usually the overall silhouette rather than a single shoulder number. If you train shoulders and back for strength, posture or a style you like, that is reason enough. You don't need to chase a masculine V-taper benchmark. Measuring your ratio can still be a handy way to track training progress if you enjoy the data.

## How to Improve Your Ratio

A ratio has two levers. You can raise the top number or lower the bottom one. The findings above point to working on both, starting with the waist. The steps below are editorial training suggestions based on that reasoning, not measured outcomes.

### 1. Bring Your Waist Down First

Body fat explained more of the variation in attractiveness ratings than shoulder width did. For most people, reducing waist circumference through fat loss is therefore the higher-value change.

- Run a modest, sustainable calorie deficit rather than a crash diet. Crash diets make it harder to keep the muscle you are trying to build.
- Keep protein intake consistent so you hold onto muscle while losing fat.
- Track your waist measurement alongside your body weight. The scale and the tape don't always move together.

Endless crunches won't target fat on your stomach specifically. Fat loss happens across the body.

### 2. Build the Muscles That Widen Your Frame

Shoulder circumference depends heavily on the **deltoids** (shoulder caps) and the **latissimus dorsi** ("lats"), the large back muscles that add width under the arms. Editorial training priorities:

- **Side delts:** lateral raises in moderate-to-higher rep ranges, done with control.
- **Overall shoulders:** overhead pressing with dumbbells or a barbell.
- **Lats and upper back:** pull-ups, lat pulldowns and rows.
- **Rear delts:** face pulls or reverse flyes for a fuller shoulder from every angle.

Aim to progress gradually, adding weight or reps over weeks. Moderate muscularity was rated more attractive than extreme size, so you don't need a competitive bodybuilder's build to improve your ratio.

### 3. Fix Your Posture

Rounded shoulders pull the shoulder line forward and narrow the look of your frame from the front. Rows, rear-delt work and attention to how you stand and sit all help you carry the width you already have. Posture changes how your shape reads to someone looking at you. It doesn't change the tape measurement, so keep your measuring routine consistent.

### 4. Dress for the Shape You Want

Clothing can change how your proportions read without changing your body. As editorial styling suggestions:

- **Structured shoulders** on jackets and blazers broaden the upper line.
- **A taper through the waist**, from tailored shirts or slim-cut jackets, sharpens the V.
- **Well-fitted t-shirts** that sit at the shoulder seam beat oversized cuts if you want to show a taper.
- **Vertical lines and darker colours around the midsection** draw less attention to the waist.

{{IMAGE_3}}

## Your Body Ratio and Your Face

Shoulder to waist ratio is a body measurement, and a tape is still the most direct way to get it. Nothing in a face photo can tell you your waist circumference or your ratio.

That said, most people working on their physique also think about the rest of their appearance. One study of male college students found that men whose faces were rated more attractive also tended to have more wedge-shaped shoulder-to-hip ratios. That is a correlation in one sample, not a rule.

If you want a separate read on your face, Aura's [AI face analysis](https://app.aura-looksmaxxing.com/tools/ai-face-rating?source=%2Fblog%2Fshoulder-to-waist-ratio) can help.

- **What it covers:** visible facial proportions, strengths, and grooming and styling options. Results are organised into your facial profile, a feature breakdown and personal styling suggestions.
- **What's free:** an on-device preview of face shape, symmetry, canthal tilt and eye shape. It runs in your browser without uploading the photo.
- **What's paid:** the full AI report is part of the 30-Day Glow-Up Plan, a one-time purchase.

Any scores are subjective, photo-based estimates. They are not objective measurements of attractiveness.

## Keep the Number in Perspective

Shoulder to waist ratio is a useful tool when you treat it as a progress tracker rather than a grade:

- **Measure consistently** or the number is noise.
- **Prioritise your waist.** In the best available data, body fat outweighed shoulder width.
- **Build your shoulders and back** for a frame that tapers, without assuming bigger always looks better.
- **Ignore the decimal places.** The difference between 1.57 and 1.618 is folklore, and attractiveness ratings were flat and variable above the peak anyway.
- **Remember what the studies measured:** ratings of images in specific groups of people, not your health or anyone's personal taste.

A lower waist, stronger shoulders and upper back, decent posture and clothes that fit will move your ratio in the right direction.

faq.q: What is a good shoulder to waist ratio?
faq.a: There is no official standard. In one multi-country study of male body images, attractiveness peaked around 1.57, and ratings were flat and variable above that. The popular 1.618 golden ratio is an aesthetic convention rather than a proven optimum, so use your ratio to track progress over time.

faq.q: How do I measure my shoulder to waist ratio?
faq.a: Measure shoulder circumference around the widest point of your deltoids, then waist circumference at the narrowest point of your torso after a normal exhale, without sucking in. Divide the shoulder number by the waist number, using the same units for both. For example, 120 cm divided by 80 cm gives 1.50.

faq.q: Is it better to build shoulders or lose waist fat?
faq.a: Both raise the ratio, but in the multi-country study, body fat explained more of the variation in attractiveness ratings than the shoulder to waist ratio did. For most people, a leaner waist is the bigger lever. Training your shoulders and back on top of that builds the taper.

faq.q: Does the 1.618 golden ratio apply to women?
faq.a: No well-established shoulder to waist target exists for women, and figures like 1.4 that circulate online are not backed by solid data. Women can use the measurement to track shoulder and back training if they want to, without adopting a masculine V-taper goal.

faq.q: Is shoulder to waist ratio a health measurement?
faq.a: No. It is an aesthetic and training metric. The studies behind it measured how attractive people rated body images, not health outcomes.

An EEG study (EEG records electrical activity in the brain) found a consistent pattern in its rating task. [Larger shoulder-to-hip ratios were rated more attractive than smaller ones](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37170034/), regardless of the sex of the figure or the rater.

Other work on muscularity complicates the "more is better" reading. A [paper testing why muscularity is rated attractive](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/6258161_Why_Is_Muscularity_Sexy_Tests_of_the_Fitness_Indicator_Hypothesis) found that **men with moderate muscularity were rated most attractive**. That fits the flat curve above 1.57 in the body-fat study. Past a point, extra shoulder size adds little.

Two more caveats are worth knowing:

- **These studies measure perceived attractiveness of images or avatars.** They say nothing direct about health, and they don't capture individual taste.
- **Image-based ratios may not match your tape number.** Studies typically compare body shapes on screen, while you measure circumference with a tape. Use research figures as rough reference points, not as a pass mark for your own tape reading.

{{IMAGE_2}}

## Shoulder to Waist Ratio for Women

Most online targets for this ratio are written for men. Women deserve a straight answer rather than a borrowed number.

There is [no single widely cited target ratio for women](https://bodilab.app/en/blog/shoulder-to-waist-ratio.html) the way 1.618 is cited for men. You may see figures such as "1.4 for women" on calculator sites. We could not find supporting data for them, so treat them as unverified. In the EEG study, raters judged larger shoulder-to-hip ratios as more attractive on female figures too. Brain activity, however, did not change with the ratio for female avatars.

For women interested in proportions, the more relevant shape is usually the overall silhouette rather than a single shoulder number. If you train shoulders and back for strength, posture or a style you like, that is reason enough. You don't need to chase a masculine V-taper benchmark. Measuring your ratio can still be a handy way to track training progress if you enjoy the data.

## How to Improve Your Ratio

A ratio has two levers. You can raise the top number or lower the bottom one. The findings above point to working on both, starting with the waist. The steps below are editorial training suggestions based on that reasoning, not measured outcomes.

### 1. Bring Your Waist Down First

Body fat explained more of the variation in attractiveness ratings than the ratio did. For most people, reducing waist circumference through fat loss is therefore the higher-value change.

- Run a modest, sustainable calorie deficit rather than a crash diet. Crash diets make it harder to keep the muscle you are trying to build.
- Keep protein intake consistent so you hold onto muscle while losing fat.
- Track your waist measurement alongside your body weight. The scale and the tape don't always move together.

Endless crunches won't target fat on your stomach specifically. Fat loss happens across the body.

### 2. Build the Muscles That Widen Your Frame

Shoulder circumference depends heavily on the **deltoids** (shoulder caps) and the **latissimus dorsi** ("lats"), the large back muscles that add width under the arms. Editorial training priorities:

- **Side delts:** lateral raises in moderate-to-higher rep ranges, done with control.
- **Overall shoulders:** overhead pressing with dumbbells or a barbell.
- **Lats and upper back:** pull-ups, lat pulldowns and rows.
- **Rear delts:** face pulls or reverse flyes for a fuller shoulder from every angle.

Aim to progress gradually, adding weight or reps over weeks. Moderate muscularity was rated more attractive than extreme size, so you don't need a competitive bodybuilder's build to improve your ratio.

### 3. Fix Your Posture

Rounded shoulders pull the shoulder line forward and narrow the look of your frame from the front. Rows, rear-delt work and attention to how you stand and sit all help you carry the width you already have. Posture changes how your shape reads to someone looking at you. It doesn't change the tape measurement, so keep your measuring routine consistent.

### 4. Dress for the Shape You Want

Clothing can change how your proportions read without changing your body. As editorial styling suggestions:

- **Structured shoulders** on jackets and blazers broaden the upper line.
- **A taper through the waist**, from tailored shirts or slim-cut jackets, sharpens the V.
- **Well-fitted t-shirts** that sit at the shoulder seam beat oversized cuts if you want to show a taper.
- **Vertical lines and darker colours around the midsection** draw less attention to the waist.

{{IMAGE_3}}

## Your Body Ratio and Your Face

Shoulder to waist ratio is a body measurement, and a tape is still the most direct way to get it. Nothing in a face photo can tell you your waist circumference or your ratio.

That said, most people working on their physique also think about the rest of their appearance. One study found that [men with more attractive faces had significantly more masculine, wedge-shaped shoulder-to-hip ratios](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/147470490800600311). That is a correlation in one sample, not a rule.

If you want a separate read on your face, Aura's [AI face analysis](https://app.aura-looksmaxxing.com/tools/ai-face-rating?source=%2Fblog%2Fshoulder-to-waist-ratio) can help.

- **What it covers:** visible facial proportions, strengths, and grooming and styling options. Results are organised into your facial profile, a feature breakdown and personal styling suggestions.

- **What's paid:** the full AI report is part of the 30-Day Glow-Up Plan, a one-time purchase of $14.99 with no subscription.

Any scores are subjective, photo-based estimates. They are not objective measurements of attractiveness.

## Keep the Number in Perspective

Shoulder to waist ratio is a useful tool when you treat it as a progress tracker rather than a grade:

- **Measure consistently** or the number is noise.
- **Prioritise your waist.** In the multi-population study, body fat outweighed the ratio.
- **Build your shoulders and back** for a frame that tapers, without assuming bigger always looks better.
- **Ignore the decimal places.** The data reviewed here does not support 1.618 over 1.57, and attractiveness ratings were flat and variable above the peak anyway.
- **Remember what the studies measured:** ratings of images in specific groups of people, not your health or anyone's personal taste.

A smaller waist, stronger shoulders and upper back, decent posture and clothes that fit will move your ratio in the right direction.

faq.q: What is a good shoulder to waist ratio?
faq.a: There is no official standard. In one multi-population study of male body images, attractiveness peaked around 1.57, and ratings were flat and variable above that. The popular 1.618 golden ratio is an aesthetic convention rather than a proven optimum, so use your ratio to track progress over time.

faq.q: How do I measure my shoulder to waist ratio?
faq.a: Measure shoulder circumference all the way around your upper body at the widest point of your deltoids, then waist circumference at the narrowest point of your torso after a normal exhale, without sucking in. Divide the shoulder number by the waist number, using the same units for both. For example, 120 cm divided by 80 cm gives 1.50.

faq.q: Is it better to build shoulders or lose waist fat?
faq.a: Both raise the ratio, but in the multi-population study, body fat explained more of the variation in attractiveness ratings than the shoulder to waist ratio did. For most people, a leaner waist is the bigger lever. Training your shoulders and back on top of that builds the taper.

faq.q: Does the 1.618 golden ratio apply to women?
faq.a: There is no single widely cited shoulder to waist target for women, and figures like 1.4 that circulate online are unverified. Women can use the measurement to track shoulder and back training if they want to, without adopting a masculine V-taper goal.

faq.q: Is shoulder to waist ratio a health measurement?
faq.a: No. It is an aesthetic and training metric. The studies behind it measured how attractive people rated body images, not health outcomes.
